sections: No. MP3 discarded some detail when it was created, and converting to WAV cannot bring it back – the WAV is an exact uncompressed copy of the MP3 as it sounds, but about ten times larger. Convert to WAV for *compatibility* and *editing*, not for quality.

table: Video editing (Premiere, DaVinci Resolve, Final Cut), broadcast
Telephone / IVR systems (resample in your phone-system software if needed)

list: Import into video editors that stutter with MP3.
Burn an audio CD from MP3 files.

Prepare on-hold music or IVR prompts.

sections: A stereo 44.1 kHz WAV uses about 10 MB per minute, 48 kHz about 11 MB; mono halves it. A 4-minute song becomes roughly 40 MB. If you need a smaller lossless file for archiving, FLAC is about half the size of WAV, but MP3-sourced audio gains nothing from being stored losslessly.

Each time you edit an MP3 and save it as MP3 again, it is decoded and re-encoded, losing a little more quality. Convert to WAV once, do all your cutting, mixing and effects on the WAV, and export to MP3 only at the very end. This is the standard workflow in podcast and music production, and it keeps the final file as close to the source as possible.

The WAV files are 16-bit PCM, the CD standard, which is more than enough for MP3 sources whose dynamic range is lower. Most editors convert to 32-bit float internally anyway, so there is no benefit in a higher bit depth here.

seo.desc: Convert M4A to MP3 free: iPhone Voice Memos, iTunes AAC, recordings. 64–320 kbps, batch, trim, fade, tags. Works on iPhone, Android and PC.
sections: M4A is Apple's audio format, holding AAC (or Apple Lossless) audio. iPhone Voice Memos, GarageBand exports, iTunes purchases and many recorder apps save M4A – but some Windows programs, car stereos, websites and Android apps expect MP3. Convert in seconds, right in Safari on your iPhone if you like.

steps: Drop one or more M4A files.
Choose the MP3 bitrate (192 kbps is a good default) and channels.
Optionally trim, fade or tag the files.
Press Convert and download the MP3s.

sections: Voice Memos to MP3 on iPhone

In Voice Memos tap the recording → ⋯ → Save to Files. Open this page in Safari, tap the drop area, pick the file from Files and press Convert. The MP3 is saved to Downloads in the Files app and can be shared to WhatsApp, Mail or Google Drive. Choose 64 kbps mono for speech to make the file tiny.

sections: MKV (Matroska) is a flexible container used by screen recorders such as OBS, video downloads and archives. It can hold many video, audio and subtitle tracks – but iPhones, many smart TVs, PowerPoint, Premiere and social networks prefer MP4. Converting MKV to MP4 makes the video play everywhere.

steps: Drop the MKV file.

sections: OBS Studio recommends MKV because if the computer crashes or the recording is interrupted, an MKV file is still playable, while an unfinished MP4 is usually lost. The standard workflow is: record in MKV, then convert to MP4 for editing and sharing – exactly what this tool does, without installing anything.

The main video track and the first audio track are converted. Extra audio languages and subtitle tracks in the MKV are not carried over to the MP4; if you need subtitles, keep the MKV or burn them in with a desktop editor.

MKV files can contain H.264, H.265/HEVC, VP9 or AV1 video. The tool decodes whatever your browser supports and writes H.264 video with AAC audio, the most compatible combination. HEVC decoding depends on your device's hardware support.

Long recordings can be several gigabytes. Conversion happens on your device, so it depends on its speed – a modern laptop typically converts faster than real time. Reduce resolution to 1080p or 720p for faster processing and smaller files.

A file extension names the *container* – MKV, WebM, MP4, MOV – which is like a box holding separate video, audio and subtitle streams plus timing information. The *codec* is how each stream is compressed: H.264, HEVC, VP9 or AV1 for video; AAC, Opus, Vorbis or MP3 for audio. A device can fail to play a file either because it does not understand the box or because it lacks the codec inside. MP4 with H.264 and AAC is the combination virtually every device on earth supports, which is why it is the output here. Changing only the box (remuxing) is fast but leaves incompatible codecs in place; re-encoding, as this tool does, guarantees compatibility at the cost of a little processing time.

The converted MP4 opens in the Photos and Films apps on Windows, QuickTime and Photos on Mac, the iPhone and Android galleries, smart TVs from a USB stick, and every browser. It can be inserted into PowerPoint, Keynote and Google Slides, and imported into Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, iMovie, CapCut and Clipchamp without any extra plug-ins or codec packs.

For archiving or further editing choose *High quality* and keep the resolution. For sharing, *Recommended* gives a good balance; set *Target file size* when a platform has a hard limit. sections: WebM files hold VP8, VP9 or AV1 video with Opus or Vorbis audio. They are decoded and re-encoded to H.264 + AAC, which is what Apple devices, Windows apps and social networks expect. Expect the MP4 to be similar in size or slightly larger at high quality.

Screen recordings from browsers often have a variable frame rate and no seek index, which makes some editors misbehave. Converting to MP4 produces a regular file that seeks properly in Premiere, DaVinci Resolve, iMovie and PowerPoint.
If the video is for your own website, WebM is a good, efficient choice. Convert to MP4 for everything else.

A file extension names the *container* – MKV, WebM, MP4, MOV – which is like a box holding separate video, audio and subtitle streams plus timing information. The *codec* is how each stream is compressed: H.264, HEVC, VP9 or AV1 for video; AAC, Opus, Vorbis or MP3 for audio. A device can fail to play a file either because it does not understand the box or because it lacks the codec inside. MP4 with H.264 and AAC is the combination virtually every device on earth supports, which is why it is the output here. Changing only the box (remuxing) is fast but leaves incompatible codecs in place; re-encoding, as this tool does, guarantees compatibility at the cost of a little processing time.

The converted MP4 opens in the Photos and Films apps on Windows, QuickTime and Photos on Mac, the iPhone and Android galleries, smart TVs from a USB stick, and every browser. It can be inserted into PowerPoint, Keynote and Google Slides, and imported into Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, iMovie, CapCut and Clipchamp without any extra plug-ins or codec packs.

For archiving or further editing choose *High quality* and keep the resolution. For sharing, *Recommended* gives a good balance; set *Target file size* when a platform has a hard limit. A 10-minute 1080p screen recording is typically 150–400 MB at high quality and 50–120 MB at recommended settings.

Convert one video at a time for the most reliable results on phones; on a laptop you can start the next file as soon as the previous download finishes. Each MP4 keeps the original file name, so a series of lecture recordings stays in order.
